meaning: Training a policy from its own scored attempts at a task, so it can get better than its demonstrations.
A number that scores an attempt or a step of one, for example 1 when the block ends in the cup and 0 otherwise.
One attempt at the task played out by the current policy; also called an episode.
An RL algorithm that takes small, bounded update steps from batches of fresh attempts.
An RL algorithm that scores each attempt against the others in its group, so it needs no separate value model.
A program that computes how the arm and the objects around it move, so an attempt needs no hardware.
One simulated copy of the scene: an arm, a table and a cube.
Many independent copies of the scene advanced together in one batch on a GPU.
Computing the image a camera in the simulated scene would see.
One decision by the policy and the motion that follows it; in the SO-101 vision task it spans 20 physics steps.
Running a policy trained in simulation on the real arm with no further training.
Inputs given to the policy as numbers, such as joint angles and object positions, with no image.
A plain stack of fully connected layers.
A large pretrained model that reads camera images and a text instruction and outputs action chunks.
The image-and-text network a VLA is built on.
A policy, here a VLA, already trained on demonstrations before RL starts.
A second model that looks at the current moment and predicts how well the attempt will end.
The outcome that followed an action minus what the value function predicted: how much better or worse than expected it went.
Labelling each recorded action as better or worse than expected, training the policy on all of them with the label as an input, and asking for better at run time.

expansion: RL with Experience and Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies
meaning: Physical Intelligence's method for improving a VLA from its own rollouts and human corrections.
A suite of simulated manipulation tasks used as a benchmark.
RL run directly on a real arm, starting from a few demonstrations, with a person taking over to correct attempts.
The program that runs the current policy on the arm and sends what happened to the learner.
The program that stores transitions, does the gradient updates on a GPU and sends new weights to the actor.
The record of one step: the observation, the action, the reward and the next observation.
A store of past transitions that training samples from repeatedly.
An RL method that trains from a replay buffer, so each real step is reused in many updates.
Putting the scene back to its starting state between attempts.
A person taking over the arm for a moment during an autonomous attempt to correct it.
